raw_response:
Thinking through this carefully, as myself:

I've been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life. I know the Haihe Plain — the soil, the groundwater situation, the market. At 66, I can still manage the work, though I rely more on machinery now than I used to. My son is in the city, so it's mostly me.

The rotation here is obvious: **winter wheat followed by summer maize** on the same land. It's what this soil and climate are built for. I have about 12 mu of contracted land. I'm not going to try cotton or vegetables at my age — the labor is too unpredictable and the markets are volatile.

I'll plant an improved wheat variety, probably Jimai 22 or similar — high-yielding, disease-resistant, well-suited to this area. For maize I'll use hybrid seed like Zhengdan 958. Hybrids are simply better yield, full stop.

On fertilizer: I've watched younger farmers over-apply nitrogen for years and seen the soil compact and the groundwater sink. I'll apply 16 kg nitrogen per mu on wheat across two splits — basal and topdress at jointing. For maize, 20 kg/mu in one application at the 6-leaf stage. Phosphorus and potassium applied as basal dressing only.

On irrigation: this is where I feel strongly. The county government has been pushing water reduction, and honestly, the wells are getting deeper every decade. I've reduced from 4 irrigations to 3 for wheat — skipping the late tillering irrigation. Maize gets one emergency irrigation at silking if rainfall fails; usually the summer rains carry it.

For tillage: rotary before wheat sowing after the maize harvest, and I'll do no-tillage direct seeding for maize after wheat — saves water, saves labor, saves diesel.
